The server will need its own private cryptographic key to generate the public key that was
issued to the client, but as long as it has that key, it can validate any certificates it has
issued. In this way, the server can reliably restrict access to only those clients it has issued a
certificate too. The identity verification step is a matter of process, and the owner of the
server is responsible for determining what constitutes sufficient identity verification prior
to issuing a certificate. However, once that process is established, it should have every
reason to trust certificates presented by a client, which it can validate.
Now, it might not be immediately apparent why a server would require a trusted authority
to sign its identity certificate, while a client does not. This is because of the specific nature
of client-server interactions on the internet. In almost all cases, a client is responsible for
initiating a connection with the server. The server, by design, has no prior knowledge of
when or from where a given request will be received from a given client.
For each request, the server must assert its own identity in such a way that the client can
rely on the assertion. It must be able to do this for any client, regardless of whether a prior
relationship has been established. There must be some way of validating the server's
identity for any given client and any given request. So, the job of initially validating, and
then subsequently verifying, the identity of the server is centralized to an entity all
potential clients can trust, and use as a single shared resource: the trusted authority.
With a client certificate, however, the server can reasonably trust its own public key
validation, and apply its private key to validate the certificate with the client's asserted
identity. The encryption mechanism for generating an X.509 certificate is the same,
regardless of whether it's being executed by a server or a trusted authority validating the
certificate. The only difference is where trust is being placed and why.
A client uses third-party authority because, otherwise, how could a client trust a certificate
signed by a server if the client doesn't know the server's assertions can be trusted in the first
place? The server doesn't need to use a third-party authority, because there is no trust being
placed in the client. The server is performing its own validation with its own private key.

Let IP represent the interpolation period in milliseconds, or how long the client takes to
interpolate from old state to new state. Let PP represent the packet period in milliseconds,
or how long the server waits between sending packets. The client finishes interpolating to a
packet’s state IP milliseconds after the packet arrives. Thus if IP is less than PP, the client will
stop interpolating before a new packet has arrived, and the player may still experience a stutter.
To make sure that the client state is changing smoothly each frame and the interpolation never
stops, IP should be no less than PP. That way, whenever the client finishes interpolating to a
given state, it will have already received the next state and can begin the process again.
Remember that a dumb terminal with no interpolation is always 1/2 RTT behind the server. If
state arrives but the client does not display it right away, then the player’s view of the world
lags even further behind. Games using client side interpolation display state to players that is
approximately 1/2 RTT + IP milliseconds behind the true state on the server. Thus, to minimize
latency, IP should be as small as possible. This desire, combined with the fact IP must be greater
than or equal to PP to prevent stutter, means it should be exactly equal to the PP.
The server can either notify the client how frequently it intends to send packets, or the client
can compute the PP empirically by noting how rapidly packets arrive. Note that the server
should set the packet period based on bandwidth, not latency. The server can send packets
as frequently as it believes the network between the client and server can transmit them.
This means that the latency perceived by players of games that use this type of client side
interpolation is a factor of not only network latency, but also of network bandwidth.
Continuing the previous example, if the server sends 15 packets per second, the packet period

more pleasant for the player such that latency is less of a concern.

In a networked game, dead reckoning is the process of predicting an entity’s behavior based
on the assumption that it will keep doing whatever it’s currently doing. If this is a running
player, it means assuming the player will keep running in the same direction. If it’s a banking
plane, it means assuming it will keep banking.
When the simulated object is controlled by a player, dead reckoning requires running the
same simulation that the server is running, but in the absence of changing player input. This
means that in addition to replicating the pose of player-controlled objects, the server must
replicate any variables used by the simulation to calculate future poses. This includes velocity,
acceleration, jump state, or more, depending on the specifics of your game.
As long as remote players continue doing exactly what they're doing, dead reckoning allows
clients’ games to accurately predict the current true world state on the server. However, when
remote players take unexpected actions, the client simulation diverges from the true state,
and must be corrected. Given that dead reckoning makes assumptions about behavior on the
server before having all the facts, dead reckoning is not considered a conservative algorithm.
It is instead known as an optimistic algorithm. It hopes for the best, guesses right most of the
time, but sometimes is completely wrong and must adjust. Figure 8.5 illustrates this.

Client-server computing distributes work between user-controlled machines and powerful shared servers. Servers manage large datasets and common services, while clients handle interaction, graphics, and some computation.

The arrangement evolved from time-sharing but replaced passive terminals with capable networked computers. It preserves shared resources without surrendering responsive local control.

Client-side Blazor is the 2019 preview model in which the browser downloads a .NET runtime and application assemblies and executes C# locally through WebAssembly. Interface events can update the page without a server call after the application is loaded.

Local execution enables a C# client but adds an initial download that affects startup. The source explicitly treats this hosting model as not yet part of the official .NET Core 3 release, so its statements describe that historical preview.

Client-side debugging observes JavaScript or TypeScript behavior running in the browser. It can inspect component variables, form controls, subscriptions, network requests, and changes to the rendered document.

A [[JavaScript Source Map]] allows a debugger to connect generated JavaScript back to the original TypeScript. Browser developer tools provide an additional view of console messages, source files, requests, and element state.

Client-side paging fetches a complete result set and divides it into pages inside the browser. Page changes are fast after the initial response because they do not require another server request.

The approach becomes inefficient when the dataset is large: the server still queries and transfers every row, and the client stores and processes values the user may never view. [[Server-Side Paging]] avoids that cost by requesting one slice at a time.

Client-side validation checks form values in the browser and provides immediate feedback before a request is submitted. Required fields, lengths, numeric ranges, and pattern rules can be reflected directly in the form model and template.

This improves user experience but is not a security boundary. A caller can bypass the Angular interface, so every important rule must also be enforced through [[Server-Side Validation]].

Cloud automation and productivity describes the value created when readily available computing services let organizations automate work without first building a full infrastructure estate. Applications, information, and workflows can be provisioned as recurring operating services.

Automation can remove manual delay and let people concentrate on the organization's main work. It can also displace existing tasks and create dependency on remote services, so productivity gains should be evaluated alongside workforce, continuity, and control effects.

Cloud billing and reporting translate measured service use into statements that consumers can understand and reconcile with contracts. Reports should connect price units, usage, service performance, and time periods rather than presenting an unexplained total.

Common processes and formats make costs from several providers easier to consolidate and compare. Frequent reporting also lets consumers detect unexpected demand or a misconfigured service before the cost grows unnoticed.

Cloud bursting moves excess work from one cloud to capacity supplied by another when the first cloud cannot meet demand. It extends elasticity across a cloud or provider boundary rather than only adding resources inside one pool.

The secondary service must be compatible enough to accept the work, data, and control state. Contracts, security, performance, and [[Cloud Service Interoperability]] therefore determine whether bursting can occur automatically without breaking the original service commitment.

Cloud compliance is adherence to the laws, industry regulations, policies, and contractual standards that apply to a cloud service and its data. General services may face broad rules, while specialist services can inherit additional industry and local requirements.

Every interoperating component within a regulated process must meet the applicable obligations. Provider location, hosting location, users, data subjects, and service purpose can all affect the compliance scope.

Cloud computing is a way of delivering configurable computing capabilities as services rather than tying each workload permanently to equipment owned and managed by its consumer. The change is both technical and organizational. Shared resource pools improve utilization, automation makes capacity available on demand, network access separates use from physical location, and measurement connects consumption to management and price. Those properties create flexibility, but they also move important boundaries: the consumer gains less direct responsibility for infrastructure while becoming more dependent on service contracts, interfaces, providers, networks, and the rules governing remote data.

Cloud computing provides on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be provisioned and released with little direct management effort. The resources can include networks, servers, storage, applications, and complete services.

The model combines [[Broad Network Access]], [[On-Demand Self-Service]], [[Resource Pooling]], [[Rapid Elasticity]], and [[Measured Cloud Service|measured use]]. [[Server Virtualization]] can help implement these properties, but virtualization alone is not cloud computing because it does not necessarily include automated provisioning, service measurement, reporting, or billing.

Cloud demand flexibility is the ability to change computing capacity as a product or service moves through development, testing, launch, promotion, ordinary use, and decline. Each stage can create a different peak or trough in demand.

[[Rapid Elasticity]] lets spending and capacity follow those changes rather than requiring permanent overprovisioning. The value appears as both avoided idle investment and a lower chance of losing business during unexpected peaks.

Containers
Containers allow you to package your applications into an isolated environment logically separated
from other applications without the overhead incurred by virtualizing the underlying physical hardware
and the resource consumption of a full-on operating system. Whether it is Windows or Linux, the
operating system consumes resources that take away from your capacity.
Containers use two Linux kernel primitives: namespaces and control groups. These constructs allow the
container runtime to set up an isolated environment within the Linux operating system. Namespaces
are all about isolation, which allows us to split the operating system into multiple virtual operating
systems with their own process tree, root filesystem, user, and so on. Each container might feel like
a regular operating system, but it’s not. Control groups police the allocation of the host system’s
resources—including CPU, memory, and disk I/O—to ensure that the actual physical server is not
overwhelmed by resources consumed by the containers.
The last component that enables containers is a layered filesystem. This is similar to how we used to
build VM images—only with better isolation between layers. When we build a VM layer, when we
apply changes to and create a new VM image, we can no longer sort out the base layer from the top
layer. Containers can apply filesystem layers that contain only the differences between the lower layers.
This approach creates an extremely compact and highly efficient way of layering changes onto each
container image to compose the final filesystem that the container operates on—with the topmost
layer being writable by the container itself.

systems and resource allocations for each instance, containers directly leverage the host system’s

more efficiently. This allows us to create higher-density workloads—thus reducing the waste of valuable

Cloud price flexibility is the ability to change pricing arrangements as demand, volume, and circumstances evolve. A consumption model may suit a small or irregular workload, while a volume, tiered, or performance model may become more valuable as use grows.

The consumer can seek a different plan from the same provider or move to another provider when interoperability permits. The value comes from avoiding a permanently fixed cost structure that no longer matches the workload.

Cloud profit margin is the portion of business value left after the costs of delivering a cloud-supported product or service. Shared provider scale, reusable services, and lower up-front infrastructure can move the break-even point and reduce some delivery costs.

The margin is not guaranteed by adopting cloud technology. Service price, integration work, support, risk, demand, and the revenue actually enabled must all be included when comparing cloud delivery with an owned environment.

Cloud service aggregation combines comparable cloud cells or services into a larger service. Replicas can share demand, operate from different data centers, or be supplied by different providers while presenting one capability to the consumer.

Aggregation supports elasticity, cloud bursting, continuity, and reuse. Because the components are intended to fulfill the same role, their interfaces and service commitments need to be compatible enough for work to move between them.

Cloud service commoditization turns computing capabilities into standardized services that can be selected and purchased with less specialist knowledge. Reusable offerings, measurable units, common patterns, and provider competition make infrastructure and software resemble other utilities.

Standardization can lower cost and speed procurement, but it can also concentrate supply and hide meaningful differences. Interoperability and transparent service commitments are required before apparently comparable services can be substituted safely.

Cloud service composition combines distinct cloud services or cells into a new service. Unlike [[Cloud Service Aggregation]], the components perform different functions that contribute to the whole.

Standardized interfaces, requirements, and management characteristics make components reusable across compositions. Changes to a standard cell must be tested in every composite service that uses its replicas because one update can affect several contexts.

Cloud service continuity preserves a useful service when its primary provider or capacity becomes unavailable. A secondary service can support disaster recovery or accept overflow demand when the first service cannot satisfy its commitment.

Continuity across clouds requires compatible interfaces, data, processes, security, and control transfer. [[Cloud Bursting]] can automate part of the switch, but it must be exercised before a disruption to show that the secondary service is genuinely usable.

Cloud service encapsulation places one or more cloud services inside a larger service boundary. Consumers of the larger service can depend on what a component does without needing every detail of how that component is built.

The book distinguishes two forms: [[Cloud Service Aggregation]] for comparable repeated components and [[Cloud Service Composition]] for distinct cooperating components. Both can improve reuse and provisioning speed when their interfaces are standardized.

Cloud service integration coordinates several delivered services so that they form a consistent portfolio for a business. It connects providers with one another and connects their services to the organizational units that consume them.

Integration includes more than exchanging application data. Contracts, service levels, identity, monitoring, reports, and bills may also need common forms so the combined service can be operated and evaluated as a whole.

Cloud service interoperability is the capability to use the same or similar services across different cloud providers and to make cooperating services work together. Its scope includes data, processes, security, governance, monitoring, billing, reporting, and service management as well as technical protocols.

Interoperability enables provider substitution, federation, cloud bursting, and continuity. It requires common interfaces and compatible commitments rather than assuming that two services with similar marketing names can exchange work seamlessly.

Cloud service requirements state the capabilities and constraints against which a service and provider will be evaluated. Functional requirements include maturity, features, interoperability, and the usage model; nonfunctional requirements include security, availability, resilience, and network capacity.

Business requirements cover pricing and value, risk, continuity, support, reporting, and billing. Turning these needs into measurable commitments prevents a technology label from substituting for evidence that the service fits its intended purpose.

The comparison should include the consequences of leaving as well as the experience of joining. A provider that scores well on current features may still be unsuitable if data cannot be exported or an equivalent service cannot take over.

Cloud-based collaboration provides shared documents, messaging, email, conferencing, and other group communication through network-hosted services. It shifts the center of collaboration from software installed on one operating system to services reachable across devices and locations.

The model supports distributed work but makes provider dependency and shared information security central concerns. Independent backups and open file formats can reduce the cost of losing or changing the collaboration provider.

Cloud-based office productivity delivers word processing, spreadsheets, presentations, and related tools as hosted applications. Users can work from different devices, store documents remotely, and collaborate on shared content without distributing the full software stack to every workstation.

Central updates and reduced endpoint management can lower operating effort. Data protection, open export formats, backup independence, provider availability, and total ownership cost remain important because everyday business work depends on the service.

Cloud-enabled business scalability is the ability to expand a product, service, or organization rapidly by obtaining computing, information, and automated processes without building every supporting system first. Network delivery also gives a small organization access to geographically broad markets.

Technical capacity is only one constraint. Business processes, support, security, supplier relationships, and revenue must scale with demand or the cloud merely moves the bottleneck elsewhere.

Cloud-native development is an approach to building and deploying applications in cloud environments. A cloud-native application consists of discrete, reusable components known as [microservices](https://www.ibm.com/topics/microservices). These microservices act as building blocks used to compile larger applications and are often packaged in [containers](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/containers).

Cloud-native development and practices like DevOps and continuous integration work together because of a shared emphasis on agility and scalability. Cloud-native applications enable organizations to take advantage of [cloud computing](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/cloud-computing) benefits such as automated provisioning through [infrastructure as code (IaC)](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/infrastructure-as-code) and more efficient resource use.

Cluster analysis begins with a deceptively simple objective: place similar objects together and dissimilar objects apart. The difficulty lies in deciding what similarity means, which attributes deserve influence, how many groups the data support, and whether the resulting structure reflects anything beyond the behavior of a chosen algorithm. Data mining places this problem inside a larger discovery process. The analyst must understand the application, prepare and explore the data, select a model, evaluate the result, and decide how discovered patterns will be used. A cluster is therefore not a fact extracted mechanically from a database. It is a model produced by an explicit chain of representational, computational, and interpretive choices.

Cluster cohesion measures how closely related the observations within one cluster are. A common point-level definition uses the average distance from an observation to the other members of its assigned group.

Low within-cluster distance indicates strong cohesion under the selected metric. It is combined with [[Cluster Separation]] in the silhouette measure.

Cluster density variation occurs when some groups occupy compact, crowded regions while others are sparse or diffuse. One global distance threshold or centroid objective can split a sparse cluster or absorb an outlier near a dense cluster.

Homogeneity is always relative to the attributes and proximity measure used. A group can be homogeneous for one purpose while concealing important differences for another.

Clustering is not one algorithm but a family of ways to define and recover structure. [[Cluster Analysis Foundations]] supplies the common vocabulary: objects are represented by features, a proximity or probabilistic model expresses resemblance, and an objective or structural criterion determines what counts as a useful group. That framing matters because the same records can support several legitimate clusterings. A method that seeks compact spherical groups answers a different question from one that seeks dense regions, graph communities, correlated subspaces, or alternate views. Modern clustering therefore begins by matching the representation and algorithm to the geometry, scale, and intended interpretation of the data.

[[Unsupervised Feature Selection for Clustering]] moves feature choice inside that unsupervised problem. Without class labels, relevance must be inferred from neighborhood preservation, spectral structure, sparsity, or the quality of clusters induced by a feature subset. Filter methods score features independently of a final clusterer, wrapper methods evaluate subsets through clustering performance, and hybrid methods combine both. Feature weighting can also let a clustering procedure suppress irrelevant dimensions while it estimates groups. These methods are especially important because noise dimensions can overwhelm meaningful proximity before an algorithm ever begins grouping points.

Two classical algorithm families illustrate how different structural assumptions lead to different outputs. [[Partition and K-Means Clustering]] assigns every object to one of a fixed number of groups and typically optimizes dispersion around representative centers. It is efficient and scalable, but sensitive to initialization, outliers, and non-spherical structure. [[Hierarchical Clustering Methods]] instead builds nested partitions by repeated merges or splits. Linkage rules determine which geometry the hierarchy favors, and the dendrogram exposes solutions at several resolutions. Neither family is universally preferable: partitioning emphasizes a single economical summary, while hierarchy emphasizes relationships among possible resolutions.

[[Density and Grid-Based Clustering]] avoids requiring globular groups. Density methods grow clusters through connected neighborhoods of sufficiently dense points, leaving sparse observations as noise. OPTICS records a reachability ordering that reveals structure across density scales, while DENCLUE describes density through influence functions and attractors. Grid methods quantize the data space and operate on populated cells rather than individual records. STING stores statistical summaries, WaveCluster transforms the grid to expose dense regions, and CLIQUE searches dense subspaces. These techniques can recover irregular shapes and reduce data-access costs, although results still depend on resolution and density parameters.

Clustering-based outlier detection treats observations in very small or sparse clusters, or outside all normal clusters, as anomaly candidates. A hierarchical approach can cut a dendrogram and inspect the smallest groups.

The result depends on the cut level, distance, and clustering method. Normal points can form small clusters, while outliers can be absorbed when the grouping is too coarse.

The goal of this chapter was to explore the .Net Core framework in more detail, and, in
particular, the .Net Core DI. Three types of service lifetimes are supported: Transient,

dependency for each request. A Scoped service will be generated once with a defined
scope, while a Singleton service will be performed once for the lifetime of the DI service

wise to know the limits of the .Net Core DI framework, as well as the strengths of other DI
frameworks, for situations where replacing the basic .Net Core DI framework with a third-
party DI framework could be beneficial for an application.

2. Partitioning the Coarsest Graph: Once the graph is small enough, it is simple to apply
any partitioning algorithm on the coarsest graph. One may even try several methods or the
same randomized method several times. Some of the popular choices include graph-growing,
spectral clustering or simple Kernighan-Lin algorithm with random starting partitions. Note
that since the size of the graph is small, it is feasible to apply a slow method like spectral
clustering in order to get high quality output [105].
3. Uncoarsening and Projecting Up: In this step the partition of the coarsest graph is used to
initialize partitions on fi ner (bigger) graph. This is called “projecting up”. Since each vertex in
fi ner graph can be traced to a vertex in the coarser graph, assigning the vertices of fi ner graph
to appropriate partitions is simple once we have the partition on the coarser graph. The fi ner
connectivity given by uncoarsening is used to re fi ne the partition. This is done using some
local search, or some variants of Kernighan-Lin algorithm (Metis [86]) or weighted kernel
k-means (Graclus [42]) [131, 105]. This step is continued until the original graph has been
reached.
Metis [86] supports different matching schemes for the coarsening step including RM and HEM.
For partitioning the coarsest graph, Metis implements four different schemes: three based on graph-
growing heuristics and one based on spectral bisection. During the uncoarsening phase, Metis uses
the K/L algorithm [57] as a partition re fi nement algorithm. Since the K/L algorithm can take many
iterations before converging, Metis also implements Greedy Re fi nement (GR) that performs only
a single iteration and a Boundary Kernighan-Lin Re fi nement (BKLR) that allows swapping only
vertices that are along the boundary of the bisection. More detailed discussion about Metis can be
found in [86].
Graclus [42] generalizes the coarsening process of Metis to a max-cut coarsening procedure to
make it effective for a wider range of objectives. For clustering the coarsest graph, three base clus-
tering approaches are explored—the extremely ef fi cient region-growing algorithm of Metis [86],
the spectral clustering algorithm, and the bisection method. In the Re fi nement step, Graclus uses
weighted kernel k -means. A more detailed discussion about the algorithm can be found in [42].

The GraphicsManager is responsible for most of the rendering logic. When it’s first initialized,
if the game is set to full-screen mode, it determines the current desktop resolution and sets the

the game objects.
A game object can specify in its constructor which draw order group it’s in. There are three
possibilities: background, default, and foreground. Each draw order group has its own list in

added to the world. The purpose of the different groups is to allow for specific objects to
always be in front of or behind the objects that are in the default group (which is nearly

that it only draws a particular pixel if there’s nothing in front of it that has already been drawn.

group. First, z-buffering is disabled and the background group is drawn. This group can be
used for a skybox, foe example, which is a cube that encompasses the entire world and has a
texture of the sky (or space). Then z-buffering is enabled and the default group, which contains
the vast majority of game objects, is drawn. Finally, z-buffering is disabled once more and the
foreground objects are drawn. This group allows for objects such as a first-person model to be
drawn without worrying about clipping into other objects.
